analysis.one_liner: Overrides state laws like California's that set animal-welfare standards for meat sold across state lines.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had one sponsor and no cosponsors, was never taken up by the Senate Agriculture Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop states from enforcing their own rules on livestock raised elsewhere and sold within their borders, whenever those rules go beyond the rules of the state where the animal was raised. Its stated purpose is to strike down laws like the one referenced in a 2022 Supreme Court case, National Pork Producers Council v. Ross — in practice, California's voter-approved requirement that pork sold in the state come from animals raised without extreme confinement. Large confinement livestock operations would no longer have to meet the standards of the states where they sell. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in November 2023 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Industrial livestock producers — especially large hog and pork operations — would benefit. Under the bill, a state like California could not enforce standards such as its ban on selling pork from pigs raised in gestation crates if the pigs were raised in another state with looser rules. Producers could sell into any state while following only the weakest rules on their books.

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids states from enforcing any law on livestock or livestock products sold in interstate commerce that goes beyond the rules of the state where the animals were raised, including any requirement 'not present' in the producing state's laws [S2].

The bill names National Pork Producers Council v. Ross — the 2022 case upholding California's authority to set standards for pork sold in the state — as the kind of state law it is meant to preempt [S2].

Enforcement would run through the U.S. Attorney General, state attorneys general, and a private right of action for anyone harmed by a preempted state law, and a preempted state law could not be enforced against violators [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Voters and states that adopted higher animal-welfare or food-safety standards, and the animals covered by them, would bear the cost. A state could still regulate conduct entirely inside its own borders, but its rules could not reach products shipped in from out of state, hollowing out laws that were designed to shape the whole market.
analysis.who_pays_short: States that set stricter food standards

drawbacks.text: The bill would void the practical effect of state measures passed by voters or legislatures — the bill text says its purpose is to preempt laws 'incongruent with, disproportionate to, or otherwise in conflict with' other states' livestock rules, the category at issue in the California pork case [S2].
The trigger words 'incongruent' and 'disproportionate' are not defined in the bill, which would invite years of litigation over which state laws survive [S2].

A good-faith argument for the bill: producers shipping meat nationwide may face a patchwork of conflicting state rules, and a 5-4 Supreme Court had only narrowly upheld California's law, leaving open the constitutional complaint. The bill answers that complaint by nationalizing the lowest standard rather than setting a federal one [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a real but narrow problem — producers navigating differing state rules — for the removal of the strongest animal-welfare and food standards that any state has put on the national market. It sets no federal floor in their place, so the net effect is the lowest common denominator, and the vague preemption standard would produce litigation rather than certainty.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, and the Congress ended with it still sitting there.

narrative.text: Josh Hawley introduced the bill in the Senate on November 30, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State standards like California's remain enforceable for now, and large livestock producers avoided the litigation and compliance costs of the bill's broad preemption — they keep the status quo rather than gaining the market-wide rollback they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Producers who never faced the preemption law

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee; he did not attract any cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 30, 2023 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other senator signed on, so the partisan shape was never tested; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would let confinement operations sell into states like California without meeting that state's crate and confinement standards, as long as they meet the rules of their home state. Their gain — a larger market at lower compliance cost — comes directly at the cost of state standards adopted to protect animal welfare and food safety.

The bill's stated purpose tracks the position the National Pork Producers Council argued in its 2022 Supreme Court case against California's pork sales law, which the bill names explicitly as the type of state law to preempt.

States that have adopted livestock standards would lose the power to enforce them against out-of-state products, the main channel through which such standards work. This includes measures approved directly by voters.
